name: connect
description: Spawn + JSON-RPC-handshake a natively-configured MCP server, then return its advertised tools (the `tools/list` result). The connection config can come from two places: when `config` is supplied inline, it's used directly (the JS-side MCP pool reads `~/.nexus/settings.json` and passes the full config through — the post-migration path); when `config` is absent, the C++ side falls back to looking up `serverId` in `nexus.mcp_server_configs` prefs (the legacy path, still supported during the migration window). Idempotent: connecting an already-connected server returns its current tool list without respawning. Connection failures are reported in-band (output `ok:false, error`) so one bad server can't fail pool init. Output: { ok: boolean, tools: array<{ name, description?, inputSchema? }>, error?: string }.

inputs.name: serverId
inputs.description: Opaque id of the native server. With inline `config`, this is the key the pool will register the connection under. Without it, this is the `nexus.mcp_server_configs` pref key (legacy).

inputs.name: config
inputs.description: Inline server config (preferred). Fields mirror the `nexus.mcp_server_configs` pref dict: `transport` ('stdio'|'http'), `command`, `args` (array), `env` (dict), `url`, `headers` (dict), `cwd`. When supplied, prefs are NOT consulted — the JS side is the source of truth. Secrets travel inline (env values, Authorization headers) and are written to the spawned child / the http request as-is; the JS side reads them from `~/.nexus/settings.json` which inherits the user's home-dir filesystem permissions. When omitted, the C++ side falls back to its pref lookup + secret-decryption path.
